questions.stem: A log merger keeps 200,000 entries sorted in an ArrayList. For each new entry it binary-searches the position with list.get(mid) and then calls list.add(index, entry). A reviewer proposes a LinkedList instead, because the inserts land in the middle. What happens to the merger?

options.text: It gets faster, since add(index, entry) on a LinkedList links the node in without shifting the entries after it
options.says: the link is cheap, but add(index, e) first walks node by node to the index, and that walk dominates

options.text: It gets slower, since get(mid) and add(index, entry) on a LinkedList each reach the index by following links one at a time
options.says: LinkedList reaches an index by following one link per element from the nearer end; ArrayList reads it directly and shifts with one array copy

options.text: It gets slower, since get(mid) and add(index, entry) on a LinkedList each allocate a node the collector must later free
options.says: the sampled stacks sat in node(int), the walk to the index, not in allocating nodes

options.text: It gets faster, since get(mid) on a LinkedList starts its search from whichever end is nearer the index
options.says: starting from the nearer end still walks up to half the list per call; the run showed ArrayList about 30 times faster for middle inserts

origin.section: LinkedList Loses to ArrayList Unless You Already Hold the Position

questions.stem: A viewer records visited pages with history.add(page) on an ArrayDeque and implements its Back button with history.pop(). The user opens home, then search, then results, and presses Back. What does pop() return?

options.text: results, since pop() takes the element that was added last
options.says: pop() takes the head, and add() put each page at the tail, so the head is the first page added

options.text: home, since add() put each page at the tail and pop() takes from the head
options.says: add is addLast and pop is removeFirst; mixing them makes the deque a queue

options.text: results, since an ArrayDeque used through pop() behaves like a stack
options.says: it behaves like a stack only when elements go in with push(), which also works on the head

options.text: home, since an ArrayDeque hands its elements out first-in-first-out whichever methods are used
options.says: push followed by pop is last-in-first-out; the order depends on which ends the methods use

origin.section: ArrayDeque Is the Stack and the Queue; Stack Is a Synchronized Vector

questions.stem: A service keys a HashMap by record SessionKey(String tenant, String id). A client sends 5,000 ids crafted so that every SessionKey has the same hashCode. Compared with a map keyed by the bare id strings, crafted the same way, how do lookups fare?

options.text: About the same, since HashMap turns a crowded bin into a balanced tree whatever the key's type
options.says: the tree orders keys with equal hashes only through compareTo; for a non-Comparable key a lookup searches through the bin

options.text: Far slower, since HashMap orders a crowded bin's equal-hash keys only by compareTo, which the record lacks
options.says: String is Comparable and the record isn't, so the record's lookups degrade to a search through the bin, half of it on average for a key that is there

options.text: About the same, since HashMap orders a crowded bin's keys by their fields, and the record's fields are Strings
options.says: HashMap checks whether the key's own class is Comparable of itself; the record's fields don't count

options.text: Far slower, since HashMap recomputes the record's hashCode from both of its fields on every lookup
options.says: computing the hash is cheap; the cost is the search through thousands of colliding keys

origin.section: Colliding HashMap Keys Stay Fast Only When They Are Comparable

questions.stem: A reconciliation job collects amounts into a TreeSet<BigDecimal> to count the distinct ones. The input holds new BigDecimal("5.0"), new BigDecimal("5.00") and new BigDecimal("5.10"). How many elements does the set end up with?

options.text: 3, since the set decides duplicates with equals, which tells 5.0 and 5.00 apart by their scale
options.says: a TreeSet never consults equals; it compares with compareTo

options.text: 2, since the set decides duplicates with compareTo, which ignores the difference in scale
options.says: compareTo returns 0 for 5.0 and 5.00, so the TreeSet keeps one of them

options.text: 3, since the set decides duplicates with compareTo, which tells 5.0 and 5.00 apart by their scale
options.says: BigDecimal.compareTo returns 0 for 5.0 and 5.00; the run shows the TreeSet keeping one of them

options.text: 2, since the set decides duplicates with equals, which ignores the difference in scale
options.says: a TreeSet doesn't use equals, and BigDecimal.equals returns false for different scales; the merge comes from compareTo

origin.section: TreeMap Answers "Which Key Is Nearest?", Compares with compareTo, and Returns Live Views
